title: Center for InVivo Imaging and Therapy Shared Resources (CIVIT)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – CENTER FOR IN VIVO IMAGING AND THERAPEUTICS The goal of the Center for In Vivo Imaging and Therapeutics (CIVIT) is to provide cutting-edge imaging and image-guided therapy technologies to advance preclinical cancer modeling research. As part of the SJCCC FY2022–2027 Strategic Plan, the Hematological Malignancies Program, Developmental Biology and Solid Tumor Program, Neurobiology and Brain Tumor Program, and Cancer Biology Program prioritized enhanced animal modeling as a central requirement for their preclinical research endeavors, with the CIVIT at the center of those plans. The CIVIT plays a major role in advancing SJCCC preclinical research by offering leading surgical and imaging expertise, thereby enabling SJCCC members to readily model and survey genetic and orthotopic- implant models of brain tumors, solid tumors, and leukemias. The CIVIT works closely with the Preclinical Testing Program, an initiative of the SJCCC that provides a streamlined workflow for preclinical testing of new therapeutics. The CIVIT partners with SJCCC members to provide consultative and technical expertise in modeling and conducting experiments for their preclinical research. The CIVIT is directed by Gregory Turner, PhD, an imaging scientist and biomedical engineer with more than 20 years of experience developing preclinical- imaging methods. Turner is supported by one senior scientist manager, one laboratory operations manager, and nine highly skilled research technologists to provide imaging, surgery, and therapeutic services. The CIVIT partners with SJCCC Programs when planning and performing experiments to ensure animal studies are conducted at the highest standard. In addition, the CIVIT staff has collaborated with SJCCC imaging researchers to develop and implement novel imaging techniques that will benefit the SJCCC. During the current project period, the CIVIT was used by 50 St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital investigators, of whom 37 (74%) were SJCCC members. Thus, 25% (37/146) of all SJCCC members used this shared resource. Of those 37 members, 25 (68%) held cancer-focused peer-reviewed grants. Additionally, the CIVIT acquired new preclinical diagnostic imaging equipment to support the work of the SJCCC members during this period. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capabilities were expanded with two Bruker 9.4T MRI systems (20-cm and 30-cm bores), each equipped with Cryocoil technology, which provides clearer images with shorter acquisition times. Both machines were heavily used during FY2024. Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging has increased due to the addition of PET/MRI and PET/CT (computed tomography) capabilities in the CIVIT. The Bruker Si198 PET insert for the 30- cm bore MRI machine enables the simultaneous acquisition of both PET and MRI data. Preclinical PET and CT capabilities have been significantly strengthened with the state-of-the-art Bruker Si78 μPET-CT unit and stand- alone high-resolution Bruker Skyscan 1276 μCT system. This investment has provided SJCCC members with the tools they need to address their scientific questions and advance their research.

title: Use of Deep Learning Algorithms to Enable Evaluation of the Determinants and Outcomes of Hepatic Steatosis, by HIV Status
text:
This project will assemble the largest ever cohorts of persons with and without HIV infection who will be
classified according to the presence of moderate-to-severe hepatic steatosis based on the application of
artificial intelligence methods to clinically obtained noncontrast abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans.
The proposed research will contribute to fundamental knowledge on the factors associated with hepatic
steatosis and risk of liver complications associated with steatosis among persons with HIV and assess how
these differ from those without HIV infection. The results of these studies will inform interventions to prevent or
mitigate the development of hepatic steatosis among persons with HIV, which will help to lower the risk of liver
complications and prolong survival in this population.

title: Development and validation of efficient cognitive composite scores of digital tools for the detection of early pathophysiological changes in Alzheimers disease
text:
In this project, the applicant will identify novel features of the digital clock drawing test most correlated with
pathophysiological events in preclinical Alzheimer’s disease (AD) using machine learning and multimodal
neuroimaging and establish the longitudinal performance of the digital test. Outcomes of the project will provide
a non-invasive assessment of individual cognitive status in the context of progressive pathophysiological
events in preclinical AD. This will enable efficient and cost-effective participant screening for AD therapeutic
trials and facilitate the translation of digital testing into AD primary care settings, especially for underserved
populations.

title: Core C - Genomics and Metabolomics
text: Biomedical Research Core C (Genomics and Metabolomics): Summary The UCSF NORC Genomics and Metabolomics Core (Core C) facilitates genetic, genomic and metabolomic studies focused on nutrition and obesity research, contributing to over 100 publications (see Table F). Core C provides NORC users access to, assistance with, and training in the use of an array of sophisticated methods and instruments for genetic, genomic and, as recently implemented, metabolomic assessment of molecular pathways underlying nutrition and obesity. Specifically, Core C’s role is to support and coordinate access to this infrastructure and instrumentation for NORC users. The NORC also supports the development of novel technologies determined by a defined process to be of emerging need to the NORC research base. For example, during the past award period we augmented genomic and metabolomic offerings in response to NORC members’ feedback and implemented next-gen sequencing-based microbiome profiling, long-read PacBio sequencing for splice isoform detection and chromatin mapping using cutting-edge techniques like SAMOSA, and increased lipidomics expertise by the metabolomic core personnel. Currently, Core C supports: 1. Advanced genomic analyses including single cell RNA-sequencing, human genotyping, long-read sequencing, and epigenetic assays to study the genetic control of metabolism by NORC investigators. 2. Genetic alteration of model organisms or cell lines, including mouse targeted knock-outs/ins, conditional mutagenesis and transgenics for preclinical testing of mechanistic hypotheses related to obesity and metabolism. 3. Maintaining and generating animal models required for NORC research. 4. Newly, next-generation sequencing-based microbiome profiling to investigate how nutrition alters the microbiome and how the microbiome helps control nutrient absorption. 5. Newly, quantitative metabolomics to identify biomarkers associated with nutritional status and obesity. Thirty-two labs in the UCSF-NORC used genomics and/or metabolomic services within Core C in the last 5 years (twenty-nine currently), and 3 more NORC labs expressed intent to do so in the next cycle. This is a profound enrichment vs. Core usage by non-NORC PIs. Research empowered by this Core includes A) uncovering genetic alterations that alter feeding, metabolism or nutritional homeostasis; B) investigating how the microbiome affects metabolism and energy balance; and C) using expression profiling of samples from humans, model organisms or cell lines to establish candidate pathways involved in energy balance. Many of these genetic investigations dovetail onto hypotheses about how metabolism is regulated that are most directly tested using metabolomics. Overall, Core C lowers methodological barriers to help NORC researchers achieve the efficient and proper application of genomics and metabolomics tools. These capabilities accelerate a variety of new directions in the investigation of obesity, nutrition, food intake and metabolism. Should this Core be renewed, we will continue engaging NORC investigators to evolve our infrastructure & research modalities to meet their needs.

title: Regulation of Endothelial Lipase and HDL Metabolism by ANGPTL3
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because dissecting the downstream
pathways of a key regulator of plasma lipoprotein metabolism is expected to increase our
understanding of how lipid homeostasis is maintained and ultimately lead to improved methods
of treating or preventing dyslipidemia and cardiovascular disease. Thus, the proposed research
is relevant to the NIH's mission of pursuing fundamental knowledge that extends healthy life
and reduces the burdens of illness.

title: Trajectory and Architecture of Tumor Intrinsic Drug Resistance in AML
text: Project 1 Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a complex and genetically heterogenous disease and one of the most common hematologic malignancies. After 30-40 years without new therapies, several recent drugs have been approved for AML, including inhibitors of FLT3, IDH1/2, and BCL2. Despite improved initial response rates, none of these regimens lead to durable remissions. Acquired resistance to these agents develops due to diverse mechanisms that include tumor cell adaptation, often driven by microenvironmental signals. For the past decade, our collaborative team has employed numerous techniques, models, and analytical approaches to studying acquired drug resistance in AML – partly as a Center in the Drug Sensitivity and Resistance Network (DRSN) – the predecessor to ARTNet. We have developed the largest-to-date functional genomics platform of primary AML patient samples and implemented genome-wide CRISPR screening. Computational integration of these datasets has generated many predictions for mechanisms of drug resistance and nominated rationally selected drug combinations, some of which are in clinical trials. This analysis has led to a central hypothesis that tumor intrinsic biology can adapt in the face of therapeutic pressure, often with support from cell extrinsic signals, to undergo a multi-step process where early drug resistance is formed via cross-talk with immune and stromal cells that leads to an eventual late, cell autonomous resistant state with features of clonal evolution. For this project, our long-term goals are to optimize and translate the most effective drug combinations into the clinic for patients with AML. Our immediate goals are to understand tumor intrinsic mechanisms of acquired drug resistance. To accomplish these goals, three Aims are proposed: 1) Next-generation genome-wide interrogation of key acquired resistance scenarios – We created a panel of AML models of acquired drug resistance. These models have been generated with long-term drug exposure, sometimes with support from extrinsic cytokines. We will subject these drug resistant cells to genome-wide CRISPR screens with overlay of drugs or drug combinations. 2) Epigenomic evolution of acquired resistance – We will use protocols for expansion of myeloid progenitor cells from primary AML patient samples to study epigenetic adaptation. Using the same list of drugs and drug combinations as in Aim 1, we will profile shifts in epigenetic landscape using single-cell sequencing. 3) Atlas of intrinsic drug resistance in AML – We have expertise with broad data integration and modeling approaches. We will use these strategies to leverage our existing functional genomic dataset combined with the new data generated in Aims 1 and 2 to generate an Atlas of tumor intrinsic mechanisms of acquired drug resistance in AML. Cumulatively, we expect these innovative analyses to have a major impact on our understanding of acquired drug resistance in AML, leading to successful clinical translation of new, more effective drug combination strategies.

title: Tick Resources Core
text: TICK RESOURCES CORE Abstract: The overarching goal of the Tick Resources Core within this P01 application is to provide support to all three research projects and share reagents, materials, and new technologies with the scientific community. Requests from the community will be handled through the Biodefense and Emerging Infections Research Resources Repository (BEI) website (www.beiresources.org). BEI was established by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and has been managed under contract by the American Type Culture Collection for fifteen years. The Core Leader Dr. Jonathan Oliver at the University of Minnesota will continue to collaborate with co-Investigator, Dr. Ulrike Munderloh. Their laboratories have made substantial contributions to developing and refining techniques for mutagenesis, plasmid-based complementation, and functional genomics for rickettsial agents in addition to developing a membrane feeder system for ticks. They have contributed 22 out of 30 Rickettsiales species for sequencing in the “Rickettsiales Genomes” project and has an outstanding record of distributing tick cell lines and microbial isolates to the scientific community. Aim 1 of the Tick Resources Core will provide and develop tick-vector-based tools to support the research for all three research projects within this P01 application. Aim 2 of the Tick Resources Core will characterize the transcriptomic response of established experimental tick cell lines to infection by tick-borne pathogens and develop novel cell lines suitable for analyses of immune pathways that are activated or repressed in response to pathogens. These aims will be achieved through RNA interference by oral exposure in ticks and the development of Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR/Cas9) tick cell lines. Model organisms such as Drosophila melanogaster have a myriad of tools that facilitate the study of pathogen- arthropod interactions. They also provide critical insights to the fields of entomology, microbiology, and immunology. However, we present strong evidence in this P01 application that Ixodes scapularis ticks have evolved entirely different principles that govern microbial infection, dissemination, and immunity. Therefore, a strong Tick Resources Core is of utmost importance to support all three Projects within this P01 application. By providing existing I. scapularis-based tools and developing novel technologies for investigators, the Tick Resources Core will contribute to uncovering novel paradigms in I. scapularis-microbial interactions. This scientific knowledge has potential implications for basic and translational science.

title: Exploring the coevolutionary potential of chikungunya virus and its Aedes mosquito vectors
text:
Chikungunya is an emerging vector-borne virus that is becoming endemic in the Americas. Using
experimental evolution and functional genetic approaches, we will explore the relative importance of genetic
diversity for virus transmission and the evolution of resistance to viruses in mosquitoes. Our project will
inform strategies for developing broad-spectrum, virus-resistant mosquitoes via genetic modification, and
for developing epidemiological risk maps for chikungunya globally.

title: Neurologic Oncology Program
text: Neurologic Oncology Program: Summary/Abstract The overarching scientific goal of the HDFCCC Neurologic Oncology (NE) Program is to use a team approach to advance the understanding of brain tumor biology and drive translation toward more effective and targeted treatments. This is achieved through the close collaboration of multidisciplinary clinicians and scientists devoted to studying brain tumors and combine expertise in genomics, cell signaling, developmental biology, immunotherapy, neuroimaging, epidemiology, and molecular therapeutics. A major goal of the NE Program is to more effectively move promising discoveries from the lab into clinical trials by strengthening relationships with clinical trials consortia, government agencies, and industry. All activities of the NE Program reflect the HDFCCC’s cross-cutting Themes of Impactful Discovery (Theme 1); Effective Translation (Theme 2); and Implementation and Dissemination (Theme 3) (see Director’s Overview), and are bolstered by the resources and collaborative environment provided by the HDFCCC. Specifically, NE member research focuses on (1) improving the understanding of the underlying biology of brain tumors; predicting patient disease, response, and survival in brain cancers; and (3) improving therapy for brain tumors.

title: Project 1: Elucidating Mechanisms of Sensitivity and Resistance to Combination Antibody-Drug Conjugate Therapy and Immunotherapy in Urothelial Cancer
text:
The combination of enfortumab vedotin (EV), an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targeting NECTIN4, and
pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 antibody, recently demonstrated a doubling of overall survival compared to
platinum-based chemotherapy and has emerged as a new front-line standard of care for the treatment of
patients with unresectable or metastatic urothelial cancer. This proposal will utilize tumor and blood samples
collected from patients treated with EV + pembrolizumab as well as functional studies using immunocompetent
bladder cancer mouse models to test the hypothesis that durable responses to EV + pembrolizumab require
effective T cell responses directed against immunogenic tumor neoantigens. The long-term translational
objective will be to use insights into the immune response to EV + pembrolizumab to guide future combination
strategies designed to prevent or delay treatment resistance.

title: Exploring the membrane-related components of HIV-1 Env for immunogen design
text:
A major goal of HIV-1 vaccine development is induction of effective immune responses. This project will capitalize
on our recent structural insights on the membrane-related components of HIV-1 Env to develop innovative
immunogen-design strategies to achieve this goal.

title: Deciphering the Role of Gut Microbiome in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Using a Canine Patient-Specific Gut-on-a-Chip
text:
The role of the gut microbiome in both canine and human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has been poorly
understood because a patient specific experimental model that can reflect genetic heterogeneity and host-
microbiome dynamics do not exist. My research proposes to develop a translational, patient-specific IBD Chip
by integrating a microfluidic gut-on-a-chip and canine patient-derived intestinal organoids to recapitulate
epithelium-microbiome-immune axis. The ultimate goal is to map the intestinal epithelium-microbiome crosstalk
relevant to IBD by leveraging the single-cell multi-omics analysis while validating the findings with RNA in situ
hybridization, which may lead to a broader impact on uncovering the underlying disease mechanism and
developing new targeted anti-inflammatory drugs.

title: Targeting the endometrial stem cell niche inendometriosis
text:
Endometriosis is a common and debilitating gynecological disease affecting ~10% of women ages 15-45. Our
studies investigating endometrial regeneration in endometriosis will address the goals of the NICHD related to
the investigation of stem cells in the endometrium and to development of therapies for gynecologic disorders.

title: Genomics and Genomic Analysis Core
text: The purpose of the Genomics Core is to provide instrumentation, computational infrastructure, technical and analytic expertise, and guidance in order to broadly enable and to enhance the use of genomic analysis in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) research. Among other areas of research focus, the Genomics Core places a special emphasis in understanding of the microbiology and molecular physiology of people with CF (PWCF) in the post-CFTR modulator era. The Aims of the Core are to: 1) Provide advanced services to understand gene expression and molecular physiology of human cells that are relevant to CF disease states, 2) Provide cutting-edge sequencing and computational resources to study microbial communities in the CF gut, 3) Provide cutting- edge sequencing and computational resources that advance research on microbes and host-microbe interactions associated with CF disease states, and 4) Develop and support novel technologies to advance genomic research in CF. These aims will be fulfilled by providing UW CF researchers with consultative, production, and analytical services relevant to the following domains: 1. Transcriptome sequencing (conventional and single cell RNA-Seq) and targeted gene expression analysis (qRT-PCR). 2. Microbiome analysis through 16S rRNA profiling, taxon-specific qPCR, droplet digital PCR, and metagenomic sequencing. 3. DNA sequencing of microbes for whole genome analysis, genetic variant identification, and variant interpretation. 4. Genome-scale genetic screens using transposon mutant sequencing (Tn-Seq) and defined transposon mutant libraries. 5. New sequencing technology innovation. 6. Data analysis, management, and integration, including consultation on interpretation of genomic data and training in genomic methods. These capabilities will help illuminate the mechanisms and pathophysiology of extrapulmonary and respiratory CF diseases, informing novel strategies for the prevention, treatment, and diagnosis of those illnesses. We also aim and to understand how the administration of highly effective CFTR modulators changes the physiology of host cells, and the composition and metabolic functions of the microbiome and its interactions with host individuals.

title: Antiviral & Antimicrobial Countermeasures Discovery and Development Core
text: The proposed Antiviral & Antimicrobial Countermeasures Discovery & Development Core (herein abbreviated as A2CD2C) will facilitate biomedical research targeted toward the discovery and/or development of countermeasures for prophylactic or therapeutic treatment of human biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) pathogens or BSL-2 pathogens that mandate select agent control. The A2CD2C will enable this research using state-of-the-art equipment for small molecule (1) screening, (2) imaging, (3) liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LCMS/MS) services and (4) histology. The core will be housed within the UTHSC Regional Biocontainment Laboratory (RBL) in BSL-3 space. The A2CD2C is significant in that it provides an efficient, integrated, comprehensive platform that will facilitate studies from the initial discovery phase through pre-clinical development within BSL-3 containment. The A2CD2C is unique within the RBL network in its focus on providing LC-MS studies for infected, treated animal tissues in BSL-3 to provide much needed information of the site of exposure of the therapeutic at the site of infection and thereby providing important pharmacodynamic information required for preclinical assessment. The major mission of the A2CD2C is to maintain, improve and expand our RBL support services in drug discovery and development with a focus on drug pharmacodynamics in terms of how and how much drug exposure impacts pathogen survival. We propose three objectives to achieve herein: Objective 1. To maintain A2CD2C support services in drug discovery and development; Objective 2. To improve A2CD2C support services in drug discovery and development; and Objective 3. To expand A2CD2C support services in imaging in drug discovery and development.

title: Genomic Mechanisms of BDNF Signaling in the Brain
text:
Although neurotrophins, such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), play an essential role in neural circuit
development and function, little is known about how neurotrophin-regulated transcription influences experience-
dependent plasticity in the brain. This study seeks to characterize the genomic mechanisms by which BDNF
regulates the maturation of inhibition within the mouse visual cortex. By identifying specific transcription factors
and target genes that mediate the genomic response to BDNF in the brain, this proposal will provide novel
insights into the etiology of neurological disorders that display a loss of BDNF production, including Alzheimer’s
and Huntingtin’s disease.

title: Mechanisms of lipid-induced bioenergetic stress in muscle
text:
Relevance
Obesity, diabetes and closely related metabolic disorders are associated with impaired energy metabolism and
damage to intracellular engines known as mitochondria. Dysfunction of these engines can contribute to elevated
blood sugar levels, heart failure and diminished exercise tolerance. This project examines processes responsible
for maintaining mitochondrial health and resilience in skeletal muscle and heart to promote physical fitness and
defend against metabolic diseases.

title: Nanowired hypoimmunogenic hPSC cardiac organoids for heart repair
text:
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. The goal for
the proposed research is to develop nanowired, hypoimmunogenic hPSC cardiac organoids to provide “off-the-
shelf” therapeutics for heart repair.

title: RR&D Research Career Scientist Award Application
text:
Dr. Cooper is a world leading rehabilitation engineer. He is a US Army veteran with spinal cord injuries
who has dedicated his career to helping veterans to lead full and rewarding lives through engineering and
advancing assistive technology. He has made broad contributions to science, engineering, and education
applied to improving the quality of life of veterans with disabilities, and providing opportunities to
become scientists and engineers. His research activities focus on the design, engineering, and evaluation
of mobility devices, robots, and other systems for veterans with disabilities. Dr. Cooper is Director of the
VA Rehabilitation Research & Development Center for Wheelchairs and Assistive Robotics, and a VA
Senior Research Career Scientist. He has built research collaborations and provided training to >4,000
clinicians/scientists. His work has resulted in four books, >30 patents awarded/pending, and >100
inventions/innovations. His work engages veterans from concept to deployment.

title: Modeling Hearing and Balance Disorders in Mice: The HEar@Jax Workshop
text:
The “Modeling Hearing and Balance Disorders in Mice: The HEar@JAX Workshop” highlights the unique
strengths of the laboratory mouse as a model to study human auditory and vestibular function in both health and
disease. Animal models are essential for developing effective new therapies for hearing loss and balance
disorders. Explaining and demonstrating how mice contribute to this goal is also key for accurate understanding
and support of animal research.
